title: Conditionals
examples: When do I use the second conditional?
What is the difference between the first and second conditional?
Can I mix different types of conditionals?

explain.say: Today we are learning about conditional sentences. These sentences talk about possibilities. They use 'if' to set up a condition.

items: If it rains, the ground gets wet.
If I study, I will pass the test.

draw.text: If + present simple, ... will + base verb

explain.say: This is the zero conditional. We use this for facts that are always true. If we do this, this always happens.

items: If you heat ice | it melts
If water reaches one hundred degrees | it boils

explain.say: Next is the first conditional. We use this for real possibilities in the future. If this happens, something else will happen.

items: we will go to the park

draw.text: First Conditional: If + present, will + base verb

explain.say: The second conditional talks about imaginary or unlikely present situations. If I had time, I would visit the museum.

draw.text: Second Conditional: If + past simple, would + base verb

explain.say: The third conditional looks back at the past. It talks about things that did not happen. If I had studied, I would have passed.

items: you would have caught the bus

draw.text: Third Conditional: If + past perfect, would have + past participle

explain.say: We can mix these types of conditionals too. For example, if I had studied, I would be passing now.

draw.text: Mixed Conditionals: Past condition, present result

faq.q: What is the difference between the first and second conditional?
faq.a: The first conditional talks about real possibilities in the future. The second conditional talks about things that are unlikely or imaginary now.
asks: Is the second conditional for wishes?

faq.q: Do I always use 'if' in a conditional sentence?
faq.a: Not always. Sometimes the 'if' clause comes after the main clause. The meaning stays the same.
asks: Can I start with the result clause?
Does word order change the meaning?

faq.q: What is the structure for the third conditional?
faq.a: The structure is 'if' plus the past perfect tense, followed by 'would have' plus the past participle.
asks: How do I form the past perfect?
Does the third conditional talk about the past?

faq.q: What does 'would' mean in the second conditional?
faq.a: It suggests a hypothetical result. It means something that would happen if the condition were true.
asks: Is 'would' always used in the result clause?

faq.q: What is the zero conditional used for?
faq.a: It is used for general truths or scientific facts that are always true, like how water behaves.
asks: Is this for habits or facts?
Can I use it for general rules?

facts: The zero conditional describes scientific facts or habits.
The first conditional discusses real possibilities in the future.
The second conditional describes unreal or unlikely present situations.
The third conditional talks about hypothetical situations in the past.

quiz.say: If the sun shines tomorrow, we to the beach.
quiz.why: This is a real possibility in the future, so we use the first conditional structure.

wrong.0: This is missing the necessary auxiliary verb for the future result.
wrong.2: This suggests the trip is imaginary, which is not the case here.
wrong.3: This uses the past tense, which is incorrect for a future possibility.

quiz.say: If the alarm had sounded, the students evacuated.
quiz.why: This talks about a past situation that did not happen, requiring the third conditional.

wrong.1: This is for present or future unreal situations.
wrong.2: The past participle form of 'go' is 'gone', not 'go'.
wrong.3: This is missing the necessary 'would have' structure entirely.
